transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2026-05-12 16:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Maria Chen (Redwood AE), Devon Park (Redwood SE), Liam O'Connor (AvalonPay CTO), Priya Desai (AvalonPay Head of ML), Michael Reyes (AvalonPay Infra Lead)
Shared artifacts: Pricing deck (redwood.com/decks/avalonpay-pricing), Security pack (redwood.com/sec/avalonpay-soc2), benchmark spreadsheet (link shared in chat)

[00:00] Maria: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — I'm Maria from Redwood, AE on this account. With me is Devon, our SE. How's everyone doing?
[00:07] Liam: Good, thanks. Liam here. Busy day but excited to talk dedicated capacity.
[00:11] Priya: Hi all, Priya. We're specifically evaluating options for reserved GPUs for our realtime fraud models.
[00:16] Michael: Michael here — I'll be owning infra questions.
[00:19] Devon: Great, quick agenda: understand your workloads, isolation/data needs, burst and scaling expectations, and then we can map to Redwood Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private and next steps.
[00:27] Liam: Sounds good.

[02:00] Priya: To kick off — our main use case is a low-latency fraud scoring model, transformer-based, 3B-ish params, about 1k tokens per request in worst case, more typically 200-400. We do both realtime scoring in API path and batch re-scores. p95 target for realtime is ~120ms end-to-end. Right now we're on our own GPUs but cost is spiking.
[02:25] Devon: Ok, p95 120ms — that's helpful. Are you using KV cache or streaming outputs today?
[02:33] Priya: We don't have a KV cache implemented today, it's a fairly naive infra. We do partial caching on our side for user profiles, but not model prefix caching.
[02:40] Maria: And what are your current throughput numbers? RPS?
[02:44] Priya: Peak is ~180 RPS for scoring, sustained closer to 40 RPS. Spiky during business hours, bursts up to 250 for short periods.

[05:10] Michael: Another constraint — data residency. Payment data must stay in us-east-1 and logs need to go to our SIEM. We need KMS integration and audit logs; SOC2 is table stakes.
[05:25] Maria: Totally understood. Dedicated gives you isolated GPU pools in your region and we can integrate with customer-managed KMS and S3 for logs. For on-prem or fully private we'd look at Redwood Private which gives a private control plane.
[05:38] Liam: Cost profile — are we paying for reserved GPUs even during low usage? How does burst capacity work?
[05:45] Devon: Short answer: Dedicated is reserved capacity — you commit to a pool. We offer configurable burst policies: short-term burst to shared capacity or to higher-power instances for a limited time. Billing can be flat for reserved plus overage for burst. We can also recommend autoscaling policies to keep effective cost down.

[08:20] Priya: What about performance tuning — quantization, kernel selection? We saw weird behavior on some runtimes with low-latency reqs.
[08:30] Devon: Our runtime does kernel selection and supports quantization paths — int8 and some fp16 fused kernels. There's always a tradeoff between latency and quality; we can run evals on your prompt sets to show token-level latency vs quality metrics. Sometimes small seq-length optimizations and KV caching cut p95 dramatically.
[08:47] Liam: If we pin model versions for production, will rollouts be easy? We want canaries.
[08:52] Maria: Yes — Redwood Dedicated supports rollout policies including canary, A/B, automatic fallback to hosted-compatible variants if Dedicated capacity is exhausted.

[12:05] Michael: For network — we need VPC peering and strict control plane isolation. How is Private different from Dedicated?
[12:12] Devon: Dedicated is Redwood-managed infra reserved for you in the cloud with VPC peering and private networking; control plane is still Redwood-hosted but with tenant isolation. Private gives you a customer-controlled control plane (VPC or on-prem) — better for regulated workloads that can't tolerate external control planes.
[12:28] Michael: So Private is probably overkill unless legal insists.
[12:31] Liam: Agreed. We want to start with Dedicated and maybe evaluate Private later if audits demand it.

[15:00] Priya: How do you handle KV cache invalidation for realtime scoring? We have per-user session prefixes that change frequently.
[15:08] Devon: We support prefix and per-key invalidation APIs. For your workload, a hybrid approach often helps — cache common prefixes (user-profile embeddings) and bypass cache for highly dynamic parts. We'll capture your workload distribution in the benchmark.

[18:40] Priya: Benchmarks — what do you need from us?
[18:45] Devon: Ideally: sample request payloads, token distributions (min/avg/max), concurrency patterns, p95 target, and a couple of representative prompts. We'll run benchmarks on a mirror of Dedicated capacity and provide latency/cost breakdowns.
[18:58] Priya: We'll pull those together.

[21:10] Liam: Security checklist — SSO/SAML, RBAC, KMS integration, audit logs, encryption at rest and in transit, SOC2 or ISO. Any showstoppers?
[21:22] Maria: We have SOC2 Type II, SSO/SAML, RBAC in the console, KMS integrations and audit logs. We'll share the security pack; if you need penetration test reports we can provide references.
[21:34] Michael: Is there any customer data seen by Redwood support? We need to ensure redaction or data masking options.
[21:40] Devon: Support access is role-based and can be restricted. For extra assurance we can set up an enterprise support process for access control and provide dataset redaction guidance.

[26:00] Priya: Pricing model — how granular are the SKUs? Are we committing to GPU count or throughput?
[26:08] Maria: Commitments are typically in GPU-equivalent units (e.g., number of T4/V100/A100 pools depending on region and model family). We provide expected throughput and latency targets per SKU. There's a monthly reserved fee and burst/overage pricing. We'll send the SKU sheet.
[26:26] Liam: For forecasting — do you provide traffic shaping or throttling to guarantee SLOs?
[26:31] Devon: Yes — you can set per-route rate limits and priority routing, and we support fallback policies to hosted tiers. That helps protect latency SLOs under bursty traffic.

[30:15] Priya: Any gotchas for long-context models? We plan to evaluate a 16k context variant later.
[30:23] Devon: Longer context increases memory/KV pressure and can change kernel selection. For 16k we recommend a mix of quantization and higher-memory instances. We'll include guidance in the benchmark. Also note that batch sizes for long context often must be reduced to meet latency targets.

[33:50] Michael: Integration — how fast can we be live? We want a pilot in ~2 weeks.
[33:57] Maria: Typical pilot timeline: 1) Contract/PO + infra prep (1 week), 2) Benchmark run (1 week), 3) Pilot validation and minor tuning (1 week). If legal is quick you could start benching in two weeks.
[34:12] Liam: OK that's promising.

[37:20] Priya: On-call/support expectations during pilot — do we get an SE assigned?
[37:26] Maria: Yes, pilots come with an SE and success manager. For Dedicated pilots we can provide 24/7 concierge support at premium.

[40:05] Devon: Quick note on quality regressions — we support eval runs tied to prompt sets and can alert on regressions post-rollout. That may be useful for your fraud models.
[40:15] Priya: Definitely. We need regression alerts to know if a quantized model drifts.

[44:00] Liam: Competitors — we've had calls with OpenAI and Anthropic. Their hosted offering is straightforward but costs us more; self-hosting is a bigger ops lift. We're trying to balance ops vs cost.
[44:14] Maria: That's a familiar tradeoff. Redwood aims to give the middle ground — lower cost than pure hosted, less ops than self-hosting.

[47:30] Michael: Any SLA numbers for Dedicated?
[47:35] Maria: We provide SLA commitments on uptime for Dedicated (monthly uptime %), and latency targets per SKU — exact numbers depend on the reserved commit. We'll include SLA terms in the pricing doc.

[50:10] Devon: Recap — action items: we'll send pricing/sku sheet, benchmark spreadsheet and scripts, and security pack. You (AvalonPay) will provide sample workloads and token distributions and confirm a pilot week.
[50:25] Priya: Sounds good. We'll aim to get you the artifacts by Monday.
[50:30] Liam: Let's tentatively schedule the pilot to start 2026-05-25.

[51:00] Maria: Thanks all, we'll follow up with the doc bundle and calendar invites.
[51:06] Liam: Thanks.
[51:08] Priya: Bye.
[51:09] Michael: Bye.

End of transcript.

Notes about transcription: occasional mishears (Redwood Dedicate / Reedwood), speaker labels fairly accurate. Meets typical Fireflies export style with header, optional sections, and timestamped transcript.
